title: Rainbow Falls on the Wailuku River, Hilo, Hawaii, USA
desc: Water, sunlight and lush greenery come together at Rainbow Falls in Hilo, on Hawaii's Big Island. Here, the Wailuku River plunges around 24 metres over a lava ledge, sending mist into the air as it reaches the pool below. On sunny mornings, that mist can catch the light and produce the colourful rainbows that gave the falls their name. Known in Hawaiian as Waiānuenue, meaning 'rainbow water', this striking waterfall is surrounded by tropical vegetation and has a special place in Hawaiian legend.

title: Sunset Point, Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah, USA
desc: Snow transforms Bryce Canyon National Park, blanketing the landscape in white while its fiery orange-red hoodoos rise above the snowy terrain. Seen from Sunset Point, one of the park's most famous overlooks, these fantastical shapes are part of the Claron Formation, whose limestone was deposited about 50 million years ago and later shaped by weathering and erosion. Because much of the park rises above 2,440 metres, snow can arrive as early as October. In today's image, snow clings to the canyon's ridges and spires while mist drifts across the cliffs, creating an iconic winter scene in the American Southwest.

title: Red squirrel in Cairngorms National Park, Highlands, Scotland
desc: As Britain's only native squirrel species, red squirrels thrive in Scotland's Cairngorms National Park. An important refuge, the park offers ancient Caledonian pine forests and newer conifer woodlands, with plentiful habitat and food for squirrels foraging for Scots pine seeds, nuts and other tasty morsels year-round. In today's image, a red squirrel is perched amid warm orange and yellow leaves, looking right at home as it ponders its next move in the Scottish Highlands.

title: Fiddlehead fern
desc: Today's image shows the gradual coiling of a young fiddlehead's tip, echoing the geometric patterns seen throughout nature. In math, the Fibonacci sequence follows a similar progression, each number formed by adding the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and so on. Today is Fibonacci Day, celebrated on November 23 because the date's numbers (11, 23) reflect the sequence. Eventually the young fern frond shown here will unfurl as it grows, but elsewhere in the plant world, the sequence will continue to appear in the spiralling arrangements of sunflower heads, pinecones, succulents and pineapples.
main_text: The Fibonacci sequence was popularized through a 13th-century math problem about multiplying rabbits.

title: The chapel and hermitage of Santa Justa in Cantabria, Spain
desc: Tucked into the cliffs of northern Spain's rugged coastline, the 16th-century Hermitage of Santa Justa seen in today's image overlooks the crashing waves of the Cantabrian Sea. Built partly into the rock and associated with relics of Saints Justa and Rufina, the small chapel eventually became a pilgrimage site, its sheltered stone walls creating a remarkable contrast with the powerful waves and rocky cliffs surrounding it.

title: Nice, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France
desc: Bathed in a sun-kissed glow, Nice is a patchwork of terracotta rooftops, historic churches and pastel façades along the French Riviera, as seen in today's image. Founded by ancient Greeks and long connected to the Italian royal House of Savoy, Nice officially became part of France in 1860. Today, that layered past remains visible throughout the coastal city in the south of France, where old-world architecture meets the blue Mediterranean waters and sunlit hills of the Côte d'Azur.

title: Diving humpback whale, Kvaloya, Troms, Northern Norway
desc: Off the coast of Kvaløya in Troms, Northern Norway, humpback whales move through the cold Arctic waters in search of a proper feast. They visit this region during the winter months, following migrating herring into the fjords. Humpbacks are famous for bubble-net feeding, a remarkable hunting technique in which whales blow rings of bubbles to corral fish before lunging upward, open-mouthed, to catch their prey. In today's image, a humpback slips beneath the icy waves under a glowing pastel sky, capturing a moment of tranquility in Norway's wild north.

title: The "Body of Knowledge" sculpture by Jaume Plensa at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany
desc: It's World Philosophy Day, when big thinkers gather to discuss life's eternal mysteries. To celebrate, today's image features the "Body of Knowledge" sculpture at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany, which molds steel letters from eight different alphabets into a human form. Spanish artist Jaume Plensa explains: "Our body is the home of the spirit. The place in which ideas live." On World Philosophy Day, we're all encouraged to look beyond easy answers and explore the questions that shape us, and the world around us.

title: Pair of barn owls
desc: These barn owls, bathed in evening light, are waiting for the hunt to begin. As night falls, these birds of prey swoop into action, listening for tiny movements in grass or leaves made by mice and voles. Their heart-shaped faces help funnel sound into some of the sharpest ears in the animal kingdom. This allows them to locate their prey with pinpoint precision in the dark before swooping silently, their soft feathers muffling their approach. In fall, young barn owls strike out to find their own territories. As the nights grow longer, you might spot them earlier in the evening, gliding over fields in search of dinner.
main_text: Barn owls don't hoot; they make eerie, screeching noises, which might explain their reputation as harbingers of doom.

title: Trail of the Cedars, Glacier National Park, Montana, USA
desc: It's time to breathe in that crisp fall air and step into the great outdoors. Today's image features the Trail of the Cedars, part of more than 1,100 kilometres of hiking trails in Glacier National Park, Montana. Its 1.4-kilometre loop includes a raised boardwalk which cuts a path through western red cedars and hemlock trees. The park boasts routes for all abilities, taking in alpine lakes, wildflower meadows, mountain passes and wilderness stretching to the Canadian border.

title: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument, New Mexico, USA
desc: Incredible views and rock-solid foundations are part of the charm of these ancient dwellings, set into the cliffside in New Mexico. Nomads had long used the natural caves above Cliff Dweller Creek as temporary shelter, but it was the Native American Mogollon people who made them their home. Archaeologists believe they created dozens of rooms inside five alcoves in the 1270s and 1280s. Up to 15 families lived here at any one time, raising children, making pottery and overlooking the fertile Gila River valley where they grew crops and hunted wildlife. For reasons unknown, the Mogollon people moved on around 1300, leaving behind one of the American Southwest's most important archaeological sites.

title: Frozen azalea with red leaves
desc: As fall's first frost sets in, ice crystals form on the leaves of evergreen shrubs, like this azalea. Long gone are the pinks, oranges and yellows of their spring blooms, but a new colourful display awaits, as their green leaves turn shades of red and purple. For the plants, the new pigments protect their leaves as temperatures drop, but for gardeners, they create a vibrant fall display, framed in white frost. When spring arrives, new growth will restore the shrub's green leaves, and the colourful cycle begins anew.
main_text: The pigments that turn azalea leaves shades of red or purple are called anthocyanins.

title: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
desc: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to the world's largest collection of skyscrapers. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters allowed the island to develop as a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth rocketed in the decades after World War II, fuelling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbour and the hills, developers had to build upward, creating this distinctive skyline. In 2026, Hong Kong has 569 completed buildings at least 150 metres tall — more than any other city.

title: Abraham Lake in Alberta
desc: Dawn's first light is reflected on the frozen surface of Abraham Lake, framed by Rocky Mountains peaks. In winter, this picturesque lake in Alberta is famous for its frozen bubbles of methane gas, trapped beneath the ice. Strong winds keep the surface clear of snow, offering winter-long views. Come spring, when the ice thaws, the gas escapes into the atmosphere.

title: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah, USA
desc: Just north of Moab, Utah, Arches National Park is home to more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches – the densest concentration of arches in the world. Today's image, North Window, is one of the best-known formations in the park's Windows Section, where towering fins, openings and sculpted sandstone create a landscape that looks almost architectural.

title: The Atlantic Forest, Brazil
desc: The Atlantic Forest is one of the world's great biodiversity hotspots, stretching along much of Brazil's Atlantic coast and into Argentina and Paraguay. Its landscape includes tropical and subtropical forests, mangroves and coastal habitats, providing a home for around 20,000 plant species and an extraordinary variety of wildlife, including jaguars and golden lion tamarins. Much of the forest has disappeared over the centuries, but it continues to play an important role in storing carbon and providing fresh water for millions of people across the region.
main_text: The Atlantic Forest is home to around 150 million people, which is roughly a third of South America's total population.

title: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
desc: Rose Island is a picture-perfect escape in The Bahamas, where lush greenery meets some of the most vibrant blue waters in the Caribbean. Located just a short boat ride from Nassau, this peaceful cay is known for its pristine beaches, crystal-clear shallows and relaxed island atmosphere. Movie fans may recognize it as a filming location from the 1965 James Bond adventure Thunderball, but today Rose Island's biggest attractions are its natural beauty and unique wildlife, including its famous swimming pigs. Viewed from above, the island showcases the dazzling colours that make The Bahamas world-renowned, with turquoise lagoons, sandy shoals and clear waters creating a breathtaking tropical landscape.

title: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
desc: Cross the Guadalquivir River and discover Triana, one of Seville’s most vibrant neighbourhoods. Connected to the city’s historic centre by the iconic Triana Bridge since the 19th century, this riverside district is known for its colourful ceramics, flamenco heritage and lively local culture. Brightly decorated buildings, traditional tile workshops and bustling markets give Triana a character all its own. Stroll along Calle Betis for scenic river views, explore streets lined with artisan studios, or simply soak up the neighbourhood’s welcoming atmosphere. While Seville’s famous landmarks are just steps away, Triana offers a unique glimpse into the traditions, creativity and everyday life that help define Andalusia.

title: Lanterns for Diwali, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India
desc: Diwali, the Festival of Lights, is celebrated by millions of people around the world, including vibrant communities across Canada. Rooted in the Sanskrit word dipavali, meaning “row of lights,” the festival symbolizes the triumph of light over darkness and hope over adversity. Families and friends gather to light diyas and lanterns, create colourful rangoli, share sweets and take part in prayers and celebrations. While traditions vary across regions and faiths, Diwali is widely recognized as a time of reflection, gratitude and togetherness. As communities across Canada come together to celebrate, the festival continues to brighten neighbourhoods, workplaces and schools with its message of unity, joy and renewal.

title: A bison in the grasslands of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota, USA
desc: One of North America's most remarkable animals, the bison is a powerful symbol of strength, resilience and conservation. Weighing as much as 900 kilograms (2,000 pounds) and capable of running up to 55 km/h (35 mph), bison are surprisingly agile. Despite being commonly called buffalo, American bison are a distinct species known for their massive shoulder hump, curved horns and shaggy coats that help them thrive through harsh winters. Once pushed to the brink of extinction, bison have made an inspiring comeback thanks to conservation efforts across Canada and the United States, making them a powerful example of successful wildlife recovery.

title: Bamboo forest, Pīpīwai Trail, Haleakalā National Park, Maui, Hawaii, USA
desc: Haleakalā National Park on Maui is home to an extraordinary mix of landscapes, from volcanic slopes and rainforest to towering bamboo forests. The park stretches from the summit of Haleakalā, which rises 3,055 metres above sea level, to the Pacific coast. More than 850 plant species grow here, including some found nowhere else on Earth, alongside native Hawaiian wildlife. One of the park's most popular walks is the Pīpīwai Trail, which winds through lush forest before reaching a remarkable bamboo grove. As the bamboo sways in the breeze, its tall stalks create distinctive sounds that add to the unique experience.

head_line: One step closer to the summit
title: Wooden stile at a stone wall, Black Crag, Lake District, England
desc: A simple wooden gate opens onto the Lake District, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in north-west England known for its lakes, rolling hills and centuries-old stone walls. This path leads toward Black Crag, the summit of Black Fell, which rises to about 323 metres and offers impressive views of Windermere, Coniston Water, and the Langdale Pikes. The route passes Tarn Hows, one of the region's most scenic spots, before climbing through a landscape shaped by nature and farming traditions. Some trails also follow Tom Gill, where woodland paths run alongside cascading waterfalls in this picturesque corner of Cumbria.

title: People rowing among colourful bald cypress, Xuancheng, Anhui, China
desc: People paddle through flooded woodlands in Xuancheng, Anhui, where fall transforms bald cypress forests into a striking display of amber, copper and rust-coloured foliage. Unlike most conifers, bald cypress sheds its soft needles each fall after they turn reddish-brown. Native to North America, these trees thrive in wetlands, swamps and floodplains, often developing distinctive root "knees" that rise above the water. Some specimens have lived for more than 1,000 years. In late fall, the still water reflects the colourful canopy above, creating a remarkable landscape that highlights the bald cypress's natural connection to wetland environments.

title: Lake Braies, Fanes‑Sennes‑Braies Nature Park, Dolomites, Italy
desc: Lake Braies sits almost 1,500 metres above sea level in the Dolomites of South Tyrol, northern Italy. Surrounded by forest and the dramatic peaks of the Fanes-Sennes-Braies Nature Park, the lake is known for its striking green and blue waters. A 3.5-kilometre trail circles the shore, while traditional wooden rowing boats offer another way to take in the scenery. The lake is also a starting point for several mountain walks, including the Dolomites' famous Alta Via 1.

title: Polar bear and cubs by Hudson Bay, Manitoba, Canada
desc: November marks an important time for polar bears along the shores of Hudson Bay in Manitoba, where they gather and wait for sea ice to form before returning to hunt seals. This annual event is celebrated during Polar Bear Week, observed in early November. Polar bears are powerful swimmers and highly adapted to Arctic life, but shrinking sea ice is forcing many to spend more time on land, making it harder to find food. The mother and cubs seen in today's image represent generations of bears that have followed this seasonal cycle, highlighting both the beauty of the Arctic and the importance of protecting the habitat these iconic Canadian animals depend on.
main_text: In a single season, a polar bear may travel more than 1,000 kilometres in search of food and suitable sea ice.

title: Black Forest, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
desc: The Black Forest in south-west Germany is known for its misty landscapes, forested hills, deep valleys, lakes and picturesque towns. Stretching about 160 kilometres, the region is home to Feldberg, its highest peak at 1,493 metres, and marks the source of both the Danube and Neckar rivers. Beyond its natural beauty, the Black Forest is rich in history and tradition. Forestry has shaped the region for centuries, while its renowned clockmaking heritage helped make the cuckoo clock famous around the world. Today, the area remains one of Germany's most distinctive destinations, blending cultural heritage with striking scenery.
